sources.newtonsPerKg: The legs' force-velocity profile, F = F0 (1 - v/v0), the force they push with at the speed v the body moves away from the bed (Samozino et al. 2008, J Biomech 41:2940), measured in squat jumps from a 90° knee by 21 resistance-trained men of 73.9-79.2 kg: F0 2820 N in the stronger ten and 2615 N in the weaker eleven, 2712 N over all at 76.4 kg (Qin et al. 2025, Front Physiol 16:1551488, Table 1): 35.5 N a kilogram. With no weight to carry in the water the legs straighten faster and push with less, as their profile says. The nearest measured push in water, a swimmer's off a pool wall, leaves at 2.2 m/s after 0.37 s (David et al. 2022, Front Sports Act Living 4:936695, Table 3)
sources.metresPerSecond: The same profile's v0, the speed at which the legs push with nothing: 3.33 m/s in the stronger ten and 2.75 m/s in the weaker eleven, 3.03 m/s over all (Qin et al. 2025, Table 1)
sources.pushMetres: How far the legs push, from the lowest point of a squat jump from a 90° knee to take-off, 39.5 cm (Qin et al. 2025)

sources.usefulWatts: The swimmer is a good trained one, not a champion, as the rower is a club marathon paddler: six highly trained competitive swimmers, compared with triathletes at the same 1000 W of the body's power, about the rower's 1040 W, spent 49 W of their front crawl against drag in the pool's fresh water (Toussaint 1990, Med Sci Sports Exerc 22(3):409-415, PMID 2381311): 41.9 N, the force that holds their speed
sources.wastedWatts: The power the same stroke spends pushing water backwards, 32 W (Toussaint 1990), a propelling efficiency of 61% against the triathletes' 44%. The arms are a blade slipping back through the water, as a paddle's is (Water.SlippingBlade): its slip is 32/49 of the speed, which with the 41.9 N fixes the blade's drag area. Taken, as every stroke of the mod, as spending its 81 W at any speed, measured at 1.17 m/s alone: it pulls about 78 N held still in the water and less the faster it goes; trained swimmers pull 92-104 N on average tethered all out for 30 s (Neiva et al. 2011, J Hum Kinet 29A:113-119), a sprint's effort, not a swim's
sources.metresPerSecond: The competitive swimmers' mean speed when both powers were measured, 1.17 m/s (Toussaint 1990)

sources.heightMetres: Mean adult man in the US, 175.3 cm (Fryar et al. 2021, NHANES 2015-2018, Vital Health Stat 3(46), Table 5), about de Leva's reference man of 1.741 m
sources.massKg: The one reference body, near de Leva's reference man of 73 kg (de Leva 1996, Table 4); the vessels' crew weighs the same
sources.ageYears: No measured reason: a working adult inside the equation's range of 18 to 70, and it moves the lungs by only 0.01 L a year
sources.fatShare: Healthy body fat at a normal BMI is about 8-19% for men aged 20-39 (Gallagher et al. 2000, Am J Clin Nutr 72(3):694-701); hydrostatic weighing of 50 men found 17.7% (Timson & Coffman 1984, Med Sci Sports Exerc 16(4):411-414)
sources.frc: Functional residual capacity, the air left at the end of a quiet breath out, in litres: a x height (m) + b x age (years) + c, for men (Quanjer et al. 1993, Eur Respir J 6 Suppl 16:5-40, as printed in Stocks & Quanjer 1995, Eur Respir J 8:492-506, Table 8)
sources.segments: Segment mass shares (de Leva 1996, J Biomech 29(9):1223-1230, Table 4); segment densities in kg/L (Dempster 1955, WADC TR 55-159, Tables 16-17, with the trunk's 1.03 for the chest's tissue since its air is counted apart); landmarks as shares of stature (Drillis & Contini 1966, NYU TR 1166.03; Contini 1972, Artificial Limbs 16(1), Fig. 7): ankle 0.039, knee 0.285, hip 0.530, chest 0.720, shoulder 0.818, chin 0.870. The arms, held at the chest while treading, stand in the chest's slab; the neck takes 0.16 of the head and neck by volume, measured in 46 women, no man's measure having been reached (737 of 4631 cm3; Young et al. 1983, FAA-AM-83-16, Tables 1-2)
sources.fatDensity: Fat tissue at 0.900 and lean tissue at 1.100 kg/L, the two-compartment model behind hydrostatic weighing (Siri 1961, in Brozek & Henschel (eds.), Techniques for Measuring Body Composition, pp. 223-244)
sources.tidalLitres: A quiet breath moves about 500 mL in an adult man (Hallett, Toro & Ashurst, Physiology, Tidal Volume, StatPearls NBK482502)
sources.atmospherePascals: The standard atmosphere, 101325 Pa (10th CGPM, 1954): air held in the lungs shrinks under the water's pressure by Boyle's law
sources.dragAreaAlong: A body moving along its length with its arms at its sides, as it jumps in feet first or glides: ten men of 75.9 kg towed 0.6 m under at 1.5-1.9 m/s dragged 94.7-153.6 N, a Cd A of 0.083-0.085 m2 in the pool's water at every speed, and 0.067-0.069 m2 with the arms stretched ahead (Cortesi & Gatta 2015, J Hum Kinet 49:37-45, head in line). They were towed head first; no body moving feet first was measured, so it is taken the same
sources.dragAreaAcross: A body moving broadside, the water carrying it across: belly-down skydivers fall at about 200 km/h (FAI), so at 80 kg Cd A is about 0.42-0.46 m2. Taken by the share of the body under water. A body moving at a slant to its length shows its length's area by the square of the slant's cosine and this one by the square of its sine
sources.dragAreaSwimming: A body swimming the front crawl, lying along its stroke: the competitive swimmers swam 1.17 m/s against 49 W of drag (Toussaint 1990, Med Sci Sports Exerc 22(3):409-415), a drag of 41.9 N, so Cd A = 2 D / (rho v^2) = 0.0613 m2 in the pool's fresh water (998 kg/m3)

sources.armourKgPerWalkSpeed: Armour is known by how much it slows its wearer, so another mod's counts too. Vanilla's full plate slows by 0.42, three pieces at 0.14, and suits of field armour tested on walkers weighed 35 +/- 5 kg with the doublet (Askew, Formenti & Minetti 2012, Proc R Soc B 279:640): 83 kg to the unit. Vanilla's full chain then weighs 7.5 kg, against a mail hauberk of about 9.5 kg (Cleveland Museum of Art 1916.1543). No mass of lamellar, scale or a padded coat was found
sources.unknownArmourMaterial: Armour whose material isn't in the table is taken as steel, what most armour that slows its wearer is made of
sources.unslowingArmourKg: Armour that doesn't slow its wearer has no weight to read; of it, wood floats enough to count. Vanilla's improvised wooden armour takes its closest, vanilla's wooden lamellar, which slows by 0.03: 2.5 kg of wood, 3.7 L of ash, that holds a swimmer up by about 12 N, a tenth of a life jacket's buoyancy. Leather and linen of the same kind weigh next to nothing in the water and aren't counted
sources.densities: kg/m3. Elements: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 84th ed. (Lide 2003), Sect. 4, lead at its recommended 11340. Steel: 77-78.5 kN/m3 (EN 1991-1-1, Table A.4). Stainless steel: 304, about 8000 (Engineering ToolBox, Metals and Alloys Densities). Meteoric iron: iron meteorites' bulk densities run 6980-7930 (Fry et al. 2018, Meteoritics & Planetary Science, doi 10.1111/maps.13067), and kamacite's is 7870-7910. Tin bronze: cast C90500, 88Cu-10Sn-2Zn, 8720 (Wieland Concast datasheet). Brass: 8400 at 60/40 and 8525 at 70/30 (Engineering ToolBox), so 8460 at vanilla's 65/35. Bismuth bronze, black bronze, cupronickel, electrum and molybdochalkos had no measure: each is the middle of vanilla's alloy recipe (60Cu-25Zn-15Bi, 76Cu-12Ag-12Au, 70Cu-30Ni, 50Au-50Ag, 90Pb-10Cu by mass) at its elements' volumes added, which holds within 1-2% for these alloys (Cu-Ni and Au-Ag are continuous solid solutions). Flint: 2400-2600, compact chert near quartz's 2650 (Miedema, Slurry Transport, Appendix A). Bone: cortical bone, 1700-2100, typically about 1900 (Currey 2002, Bones: Structure and Mechanics). Ash: European ash at 12% moisture, 680 (The Wood Database, European Ash). Hickory: shagbark hickory at 12% moisture, 800 (The Wood Database, Shagbark Hickory). A haft in the water for minutes stays dry: water enters wood through its end grain slowly. Linen: flax fibre, 1500 (Bledzki & Gassan 1999, Prog Polym Sci 24(2):221-274). Hide and leather: skin, 1090 (Woodard & White 1986, Br J Radiol 59:1209; ICRU Report 46): dry leather is porous, but its pores fill within minutes in the water, which leaves the tissue's own density
sources.alike: Every stone a tool is knapped from is taken as flint, the commonest of them; a club's 'wood' as ash; leather and every bear's hide as hide
sources.handlePrefix: A tool whose material starts with this has a handle of it and a head of the rest: vanilla's bone-handled knives and axes (bonechert)
sources.tools: Whatever vanilla's item type calls a tool or weapon (EnumTool), as a head of metal or stone and a haft of wood, each measured on a real hand-forged or traditional tool. The head's volume is its mass over the metal it was measured in; carried, it is that volume of the item's own metal or stone (vanilla's material or metal variant), so a copper head of a steel head's size is heavier and a flint one lighter: a steel forest axe's head as flint, 0.30 kg, against experimental flint axe heads of 243-482 g, median 362 g (EXARC, ark:/88735/10828). The haft floats. Measured: axe, Gränsfors Bruk Scandinavian Forest Axe, 0.9 kg head, 1.2 kg with its hickory haft (gransforsbruk.com; Dictum 705961). Pickaxe and crowbar head, 2.27 kg (Fiskars IsoCore pick head); its haft, the Gränsfors Splitting Maul's 0.80 m hickory haft, 3.27 kg whole less its 2.5 kg head. Shovel, Krumpholz spade forged in one piece, 1.96 kg head, 2.30 kg with its ash T-handle. Hoe: a medieval iron spade blade, 0.580 kg (Museum Wales), on the spade's haft. Scythe: Schröckenfux Hahn blade, 35 cm, 380 g (sensenwerk.de); its snath an ash pole of the maker's 26x30 mm section and 1.55 m, between its 150 and 160 cm lengths (Dictum 705609), 0.82 kg of ash. Sickle, Schröckenfux scythe-sickle blade 270 mm, 350 g (Dictum 706446). Knife, Mora Companion HeavyDuty carbon, 135 g whole, its handle not told apart. Hammer: a 2 lb cross-peen head on a 16 in hickory handle, 2.6 lb whole (Seymour Midwest 41572). Tongs, AncientSmithy universal tongs, 520 mm, about 1.0 kg. Sword, Albion Next Generation Knight, 1.19 kg (myArmoury review). Spear, a reproduction 34 cm socketed head, 375 g (Therion Arms), on the snath's ash. Javelin, a Roman plumbata head, 74 g (Museum Wales). Shield: a hand-raised steel boss, 485 g (The Viking Dragon), on an 80 cm board 6 mm thick (Hurstwic), 3.0 L of ash. Nothing was measured for the rest, which take the closest: poleaxe and halberd the Gränsfors felling axe's 1.5 kg head (Dictum 705987) on the snath; saw the scythe's blade on the hammer's handle; shears and chisel the sickle's blade; probe and meter the knife; drill, mace and warhammer the hammer; wrench the tongs; crossbow and firearm the sword's steel on the snath's ash; pike and polearm the spear; bow, club and staff the snath alone; a sling weighs nothing

sources.aeration: The air in the plume as a whole just after breaking: a mean void fraction of about 0.2 at 0.07 of a wave period, falling to 0.1 at 0.2 of it (Lamarre & Melville 1994, JASA 95(3):1317-1328, Fig. 6c, lab packets of 2 s period, read off the plot). The 24% measured at sea was one peak event at a gauge 0.2 m deep, 5% at 0.5 m and none at 0.8 m (Lamarre & Melville 1992, IEEE J Oceanic Eng 17(2), Sec. IV-C), so it is not the plume's
sources.aerationAfterPeriod: The same plume's mean void fraction after one wave period, about 1%, with about 5% of the air left (Lamarre & Melville 1994, Figs. 6c and A1c)
sources.plumeDepthPerHeight: Twice the depth of the air's centre, which sinks at about 0.2 wave heights a period to about 0.3 at one period (Lamarre & Melville 1994, Fig. 7b). This is the plume whose air the void fractions measure. Bubbles reach much deeper by echosounder, a mean of about 1.2 Hs at c_p/U10 = 1.2 and deeper in young seas (Derakhti et al. 2024, JGR Oceans 129(5), Fig. 10a), but far too dilute to tell on a body's lift, so the sea's age doesn't enter
sources.rollerSpeedRatio: A deep-water breaker's turbulent front advances at 0.7-0.8 of the phase speed (Rapp & Melville 1990, Phil Trans R Soc A 331:735-808)
sources.rollerSeconds: Active breaking is about a fifth of a whitecap's 5.3 s mean lifetime, about 1 s (Callaghan 2013, J Geophys Res Atmos 118:9997-10010)
